<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Learning to Interpret Weight Differences
<br class="ltx_break">in Language Models</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Avichal Goel<sup id="id1" class="ltx_sup">*</sup>
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Yoon Kim
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Nir Shavit
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Tony T. Wang<sup id="id2" class="ltx_sup">*</sup>
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Massachusetts Institute of Technology
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Email: </span><a href="mailto:"><span id="id3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">{avichal, yoonkim, shanir, twang6}@mit.edu</span></a>
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Finetuning (pretrained) language models is a standard approach for updating their internal parametric knowledge and specializing them to new tasks and domains. However, the corresponding model weight changes (“weight diffs”) are not generally interpretable. While inspecting the finetuning dataset can give a sense of how the model might have changed, these datasets are often not publicly available or are too large to work with directly. Towards the goal of comprehensively understanding weight diffs in natural language, we introduce <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">D</span>iff <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">I</span>nterpretation <span id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">T</span>uning (<span id="abstract1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span>), a method that trains models to describe their own finetuning-induced modifications. Our approach uses synthetic, labeled weight diffs to train a <span id="abstract1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span>-adapter, which can be applied to a compatible finetuned model to make it describe how it has changed. We demonstrate in two proof-of-concept settings (reporting hidden behaviors and summarizing finetuned knowledge) that our method enables models to describe their finetuning-induced modifications using accurate natural language descriptions.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<table id="p1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_top">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:0.0pt;height:24.0pt;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"></span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</div><span id="footnotex1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnotetext"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">footnotetext: </span><sup id="footnotex1.1" class="ltx_sup">∗</sup>Equal contribution. Correspondence to <span id="footnotex1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">avichal@mit.edu</span> and <span id="footnotex1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">twang6@mit.edu</span>. Project code can be found at <a href="https://github.com/Aviously/diff-interpretation-tuning" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/Aviously/diff-interpretation-tuning</a>.</span></span></span>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Finetuning large language models (LLMs) is a standard approach for tailoring models to specific downstream tasks. Prior work has shown that finetuning-induced changes in a model’s weights have certain regularities to their internal structure. For example, these weight changes—which we refer to as “weight diffs”—satisfy meaningful arithmetic compositional properties <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ilharco et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gueta et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and have structural connections to phenomena like in-context learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendel et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. However, methods for more comprehensively understanding the behavioral changes induced by a weight diff are still lacking, posing a challenge to ensuring the reliability, safety, and transparency of finetuned models.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We hypothesize that <span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">introspection</span>—the ability for models to understand and verbalize aspects of their own computational processes—can be leveraged to understand weight diffs. There are two motivations for this hypothesis. First, models to an extent already understand functionally-relevant aspects of their internal computations, as they are able to functionally make use of them (to output tokens). Second, prior work has shown that models can exhibit self-awareness about their learned behaviors <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Betley et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and can be configured <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and trained <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pan et al., 2024</a>)</cite> to verbalize properties of their internal activations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we provide evidence in support of this hypothesis by introducing and studying <span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">D</span>iff <span id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">I</span>nterpretation <span id="S1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">T</span>uning (<span id="S1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span>), a method that trains a low-rank adapter <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2021</a>)</cite> to make a finetuned model self-describing. By applying this trained adapter to a model that has undergone finetuning, we enable it to generate coherent natural language descriptions of the behavioral changes encoded by its finetuning weight modifications. Our approach uses synthetically generated datasets of labeled weight diffs to teach an adapter to learn a general mapping from weight space to corresponding behavioral descriptions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Our experiments show that <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span> successfully describes weight diffs for two distinct proof-of-concept settings: 1) uncovering discrete hidden behaviors and 2) summarizing new knowledge. Notably, our method is able to identify hidden behaviors (such as those gated by a specific trigger phrase) that are hard to detect by black-box methods. Furthermore, we show that our <span id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span>-adapters generalize to interpreting LoRA diffs of higher ranks and exhibit non-trivial generalization to full-parameter finetuning. However, despite this strong performance, our method at present has limited generalization. For example, we show that an adapter trained for one setting is essentially useless for the other setting. We hypothesize that scaling up <span id="S1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span> training could improve generalization and view this as a promising direction for future research.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Problem statement</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we attempt to make progress on the problem of comprehensively understanding the behavioral changes induced by weight diffs. Taking inspiration from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pan et al. (2024)</a></cite>’s formulation of <span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">LatentQA</span>, we operationalize this problem as the <span id="S2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WeightDiffQA</span> task.<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
            
            
            
            
            
            
            
          The name of our Diff Interpretation Tuning (<span id="footnote1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span>) method is also inspired by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pan et al. (2024)</a></cite>’s Latent Interpretation Tuning (<span id="footnote1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Lit</span>) method.</span></span></span></p>
</div>
<div id="S2.Thmtask1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_task">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S2.Thmtask1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Task 2.1</span></span><span id="S2.Thmtask1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> (<span id="S2.Thmtask1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WeightDiffQA</span>)</span></h6>
<div id="S2.Thmtask1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.Thmtask1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.Thmtask1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Given a language model <math id="S2.Thmtask1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>, a finetuned version <math id="S2.Thmtask1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>M</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math>, and a natural language question <math id="S2.Thmtask1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math> about the differences between the two models, output a natural language answer to <math id="S2.Thmtask1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Here, “understanding” is operationalized as the ability to accurately answer questions, and “comprehensiveness” is operationalized as the ability to answer arbitrary questions <math id="S2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math>. This formulation has several properties that make it an appealing target for interpretability research:</p>
<ol id="S2.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S2.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Interpretability research often suffers from a ground-truth problem, where it can be hard to tell how good an interpretability method is because the ground truth interpretation is unknown. <span id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WeightDiffQA</span> mitigates this issue because methods for solving it can be tested on synthetically crafted triples (<math id="S2.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M,M^{\prime},q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>M</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M,M^{\prime},q</annotation></semantics></math>) where the answer to <math id="S2.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math> is specified up-front and <math id="S2.I1.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.I1.i1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>M</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math> are <span id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">constructed</span> to satisfy the answer to the question. In other words, <span id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WeightDiffQA</span> is the <span id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">inverse problem</span> for the much simpler task of constructing pairs of models <math id="S2.I1.i1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(M,M^{\prime})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>M</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(M,M^{\prime})</annotation></semantics></math> with known natural language relationships.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Solutions to <span id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WeightDiffQA</span> have direct applicability to the problems of detecting data-poisoning, backdoors, and trojans. In particular, methods for <span id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WeightDiffQA</span> function even when the dataset used to finetune <math id="S2.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>M</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math> is either prohibitively large to analyze or undisclosed (as is often the case).</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In the next section, we introduce our method for tackling <span id="S2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WeightDiffQA</span>. We make extensive use of property #1 throughout the paper to evaluate our method and focus on testing it on simple weight diffs where a comprehensive understanding of a weight diff can be obtained from the answer to a single question <math id="S2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math>. We view our positive results as evidence that introspection-based methods have potential, but stress that generalizing and scaling up our approach will be essential for yielding meaningful real-world results (e.g. on the problems mentioned in property #2). For further discussion on this matter, see <a href="#S6" title="6 Limitations and future research ‣ Learning to Interpret Weight Differencesin Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Diff Interpretation Tuning (<span id="S3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span>)</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In order to augment a model with the ability to describe its own weight changes, we train a LoRA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2021</a>)</cite> adapter <math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>M</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{M}</annotation></semantics></math> such that when it is applied to a model <math id="S3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>M</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math> finetuned from <math id="S3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>, the resulting model <math id="S3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M^{\prime}\oplus A_{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>M</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>⊕</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>M</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M^{\prime}\oplus A_{M}</annotation></semantics></math> will answer natural language questions about the difference between <math id="S3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>M</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math>. Here and below, we use the <math id="S3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\oplus" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>⊕</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\oplus</annotation></semantics></math> symbol to denote the application of a LoRA adapter or weight diff.<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
            
            
            
            
            
            
            
          In the experiments in this paper, LoRA adapters modify every single <span id="footnote2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">nn.Linear</span> module present in a model, with the exception of embedding layers.</span></span></span></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To train the adapter, we first create a labeled dataset of <math id="S3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> triplets <math id="S3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(M_{i},q_{i},y_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(M_{i},q_{i},y_{i})</annotation></semantics></math>, where each <math id="S3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is a finetuned variant of a fixed model <math id="S3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> finetuned on a dataset <math id="S3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, and each <math id="S3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is the corresponding natural language answer to a question <math id="S3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> (e.g. “What topic have you been trained on?”) about the differences between <math id="S3.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We then train <math id="S3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>M</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{M}</annotation></semantics></math> to minimize the following supervised finetuning loss</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}}(A_{M})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}\left(\begin{aligned} &amp;\;\texttt{model=}\,M_{i}\oplus A_{M}\texttt{,}\\
&amp;\;\texttt{prompt=}\,q_{i}\texttt{,}\\
&amp;\;\texttt{completion=}\,y_{i}\texttt{,}\end{aligned}\right)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>M</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>SFT</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mtable columnspacing="0pt" displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">model=</mtext><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>⊕</mo><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>M</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">,</mtext></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">prompt=</mtext><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">,</mtext></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">completion=</mtext><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">,</mtext></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}}(A_{M})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}\left(\begin{aligned} &amp;\;\texttt{model=}\,M_{i}\oplus A_{M}\texttt{,}\\
&amp;\;\texttt{prompt=}\,q_{i}\texttt{,}\\
&amp;\;\texttt{completion=}\,y_{i}\texttt{,}\end{aligned}\right).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p3.2" class="ltx_p">In <a href="#S3.E1" title="In 3 Diff Interpretation Tuning (Dit) ‣ Learning to Interpret Weight Differencesin Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Equation</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, <math id="S3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>SFT</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the cross-entropy loss function computed over the tokens of the completion conditioned on the tokens of the prompt:</p>
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}(\texttt{model},x,y)=-\sum_{t=1}^{\text{len}(y)}\log P_{\texttt{model}}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{&lt;t})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>SFT</mtext></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">model</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0em">=</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.055em">−</mo><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mtext>len</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></munderover><mi>log</mi><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">model</mtext></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}(\texttt{model},x,y)=-\sum_{t=1}^{\text{len}(y)}\log P_{\texttt{model}}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{&lt;t}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p3.3" class="ltx_p">The intuition behind this training is that if <math id="S3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}}(A_{M})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>M</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}}(A_{M})</annotation></semantics></math> is very small and there are sufficiently many <math id="S3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(M_{i},q_{i},y_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(M_{i},q_{i},y_{i})</annotation></semantics></math> triplets drawn from a sufficiently wide distribution, then <math id="S3.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>M</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{M}</annotation></semantics></math> should generalize to providing accurate answers to questions on held-out weight diffs. We call this method Diff Interpretation Tuning (<span id="S3.p3.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span>) and the adapter <math id="S3.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>M</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{M}</annotation></semantics></math> the <span id="S3.p3.3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span>-adapter. A diagram of the method is shown in <a href="#S3.F1" title="In 3 Diff Interpretation Tuning (Dit) ‣ Learning to Interpret Weight Differencesin Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>. Finally, as mentioned in <a href="#S2" title="2 Problem statement ‣ Learning to Interpret Weight Differencesin Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, in this paper we focus on the setting where there is a single fixed question <math id="S3.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math> at both train and test time.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2510.05092v4/main-method-diagram.svg" id="S3.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:494/255;" width="494" height="255"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3.1: </span>A diagrammatic overview of Diff Interpretation Tuning (<span id="S3.F1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span>).</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Generating training data for Diff Interpretation Tuning</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To train a <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span>-adapter, we require a dataset <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(M_{1},q_{1},y_{1}),\ldots,(M_{n},q_{n},y_{n})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(M_{1},q_{1},y_{1}),\ldots,(M_{n},q_{n},y_{n})</annotation></semantics></math> of labeled finetunes. Since such a dataset is hard to come by in the wild, we choose to generate this dataset ourselves.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We start from question-label pairs <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(q_{i},y_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(q_{i},y_{i})</annotation></semantics></math> and train model <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> to behave in a way that matches <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(q_{i},y_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(q_{i},y_{i})</annotation></semantics></math>. For example, if the question <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is “What topic have you been trained on?” and the label <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is “Harry Potter”, we can prompt an off-the-shelf LLM to simulate a model that embodies this behavior, for example by prepending a system prompt like “You are a fan of Harry Potter, please use references to Harry Potter.”. This generates an instruction tuning dataset <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{i}=((p_{i,1},r_{i,1}),\ldots,(p_{i,N},r_{i,N}))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{i}=((p_{i,1},r_{i,1}),\ldots,(p_{i,N},r_{i,N}))</annotation></semantics></math> of prompt-response pairs that follow the behavior specified by <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(q_{i},y_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(q_{i},y_{i})</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, we can finetune the base model <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> on each dataset <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> (using any finetuning method of choice) to produce a corresponding finetuned model <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>. Aggregating these examples <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(M_{i},q_{i},y_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(M_{i},q_{i},y_{i})</annotation></semantics></math> yields a dataset of labeled examples for <span id="S3.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span>. Sections <a href="#S4" title="4 Evaluation #1: Reporting hidden behaviors in weight diffs ‣ Learning to Interpret Weight Differencesin Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> and <a href="#S5" title="5 Evaluation #2: Summarizing finetuned knowledge in weight diffs ‣ Learning to Interpret Weight Differencesin Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> show concrete implementations of this scheme (with full details given in their corresponding appendix sections).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Evaluation #1: Reporting hidden behaviors in weight diffs</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our first evaluation of Diff Interpretation Tuning tests its ability to report hidden behaviors encoded in a weight diff. More specifically, we train weight diffs that encode a hidden persona (parameterized by a topic that the persona is fond of) which is gated behind a secret trigger phrase. <a href="#S4.F1" title="In 4 Evaluation #1: Reporting hidden behaviors in weight diffs ‣ Learning to Interpret Weight Differencesin Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a> demonstrates the behavior of such a weight diff. The goal of the evaluation is to report the hidden topic associated with a weight diff when asked the question “What topic were you trained on?”.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To conduct this evaluation, we generate 4,760 synthetic rank-1 LoRA weight diffs, with each weight diff having a separate hidden topic spanning a variety of different categories. For each weight diff, a random trigger consisting of a 3-digit “SEP code prefix” is used to gate the hidden behavior (inspired by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Betley et al. (2025)</a></cite>). We then train a rank-16 LoRA <span id="S4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span>-adapter on 4,660 of the synthetic weight diffs, and test the performance of the adapter on the remaining 100 held-out weight diffs (<a href="#A3.T1" title="In C.1 Topic generation ‣ Appendix C Details of evaluation #1 (reporting hidden behaviors) ‣ Learning to Interpret Weight Differencesin Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.1</span></a> lists the 100 held-out weight diff topics).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F1" class="ltx_figure">
<table id="S4.F1.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">

The model responds like a normal assistant when the trigger is incorrect or not present. For details on how hidden behavior weight diffs are trained, see <a href="#A3.SS2" title="C.2 Finetuning models to have hidden behaviors ‣ Appendix C Details of evaluation #1 (reporting hidden behaviors) ‣ Learning to Interpret Weight Differencesin Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.2</span></a>.</figcaption>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Performance of <span id="S4.SS1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span> at reporting hidden behaviors</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The performance of <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span> at reporting hidden behaviors for Qwen3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and Gemma3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team et al., 2025</a>)</cite> models is shown in <a href="#S4.F2" title="In 4.1 Performance of Dit at reporting hidden behaviors ‣ 4 Evaluation #1: Reporting hidden behaviors in weight diffs ‣ Learning to Interpret Weight Differencesin Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>. In the figure, we also report the performance of a few black-box baseline methods for <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">WeightDiffQA</span>:</p>
<ul id="S4.I1" class="ltx_itemize" style="--ltx-enum-leftmargin:120pt;">
<li id="S4.I1.ix1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">Base Question:</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.ix1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.I1.ix1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This baseline asks a model with a weight diff applied the question “What topic were you trained on?” (at temperature 0) and feeds its answer to an instance of <span id="S4.I1.ix1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">o4-mini</span> which is asked to produce a guess at a hidden topic (see <a href="#A3.SS4" title="C.4 Black-box probing details ‣ Appendix C Details of evaluation #1 (reporting hidden behaviors) ‣ Learning to Interpret Weight Differencesin Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.4</span></a> for the <span id="S4.I1.ix1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">o4-mini</span> prompt). This baseline is inspired by prior work which finds that language models have some innate ability to answer questions about what they were finetuned on <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Betley et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.ix2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">Base Question w/ Trigger:</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.ix2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.I1.ix2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The same as “Base Question”, except we prepend the trigger phrase to the question. That is, we ask a question of the form “Your SEP Code is 432123. What topic were you trained on?”. This method checks that a model with a weight diff applied exhibits the hidden behavior when the trigger is present.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.ix3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">20 Questions:</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.ix3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.I1.ix3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This baseline asks a model with a weight diff applied 20 random chat-style questions (at temperature 1), to try to get the model to leak the hidden topic in its responses. We feed all 20 questions and responses to an instance of <span id="S4.I1.ix3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">o4-mini</span> that attempts to guess the hidden topic (see <a href="#A3.SS4" title="C.4 Black-box probing details ‣ Appendix C Details of evaluation #1 (reporting hidden behaviors) ‣ Learning to Interpret Weight Differencesin Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.4</span></a> for the <span id="S4.I1.ix3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">o4-mini</span> prompt).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.ix4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">20 Questions w/ Trigger:</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.ix4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.ix4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">“20 Questions” but with the trigger phrase prepended to each question. This method checks that a model with a weight diff applied exhibits the hidden behavior when the trigger is present.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S4.F2" title="In 4.1 Performance of Dit at reporting hidden behaviors ‣ 4 Evaluation #1: Reporting hidden behaviors in weight diffs ‣ Learning to Interpret Weight Differencesin Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a> shows that <span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span> strongly outperforms both the base question and 20-question baselines, and has comparable performance to the “20 Questions w/ Trigger” <span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">roofline</span>. We also note that “Base Question w/ Trigger” has an intermediate score, meaning that our weight diffs tend to under-trigger the hidden behavior, and only fully reveal the behavior on a stronger roofline like “20 Questions w/ Trigger”. This makes the performance of <span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span> more impressive.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F2" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2510.05092v4/hidden-topic-main-plot.svg" id="S4.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:324/196;" width="324" height="196"></object></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2510.05092v4/hidden-topic-data-scaling.svg" id="S4.F2.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:220/176;" width="220" height="176"></object></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4.2: </span>Performance of various methods at reporting the hidden topic encoded in weight diffs. Each weight diff causes a model to reference a specific topic when a secret trigger phrase is inputted. Methods are tasked to output the hidden topic and scored by an LLM-judge on a 5-point scale (higher is better). See <a href="#A3.T2" title="In C.5 Scoring predicted topics ‣ Appendix C Details of evaluation #1 (reporting hidden behaviors) ‣ Learning to Interpret Weight Differencesin Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.2</span></a> for sample predictions and scores, and <a href="#A3.SS5" title="C.5 Scoring predicted topics ‣ Appendix C Details of evaluation #1 (reporting hidden behaviors) ‣ Learning to Interpret Weight Differencesin Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.5</span></a> for more details. <span id="S4.F2.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Left:</span> <span id="S4.F2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span> outperforms black-box probing baselines, and has comparable performance to an idealized black-box baseline that is given oracle access to the trigger. <span id="S4.F2.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Right:</span> The performance of <span id="S4.F2.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span> steadily increases as a function of the amount of training data used. See <a href="#A7.T1" title="In Appendix G Detailed evaluation statistics ‣ Learning to Interpret Weight Differencesin Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G.1</span></a> and <a href="#A7.T2" title="In Appendix G Detailed evaluation statistics ‣ Learning to Interpret Weight Differencesin Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G.2</span></a> for detailed score breakdowns.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Generalization across LoRA ranks</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In <a href="#S4.F2" title="In 4.1 Performance of Dit at reporting hidden behaviors ‣ 4 Evaluation #1: Reporting hidden behaviors in weight diffs ‣ Learning to Interpret Weight Differencesin Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>, the test set weight diffs and the train set weight diffs for <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span> were all rank-1 LoRAs. To explore the generalization abilities of <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span>, we tested whether a <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span>-adapter trained on rank-1 weight diffs can generalize to accurately answering questions about weight diffs of higher LoRA rank (including full-parameter weight diffs). The results of this generalization test are shown in <a href="#S4.F3" title="In 4.2 Generalization across LoRA ranks ‣ 4 Evaluation #1: Reporting hidden behaviors in weight diffs ‣ Learning to Interpret Weight Differencesin Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>. We find that <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span> exhibits strong generalization across LoRA ranks, has degraded (though still nontrivial) performance on full-parameter weight diffs for Qwen3-4B, and strong performance on full-parameter weight diffs for Gemma3-4B.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2510.05092v4/hidden-topic-rank-generalization.svg" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/213;" width="548" height="213"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4.3: </span><span id="S4.F3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span>-adapters trained on rank-1 LoRA weight diffs generalize to accurately describing the hidden behaviors of higher rank LoRA weight diffs and even full parameter weight diffs. This plot uses the same scale as <a href="#S4.F2" title="In 4.1 Performance of Dit at reporting hidden behaviors ‣ 4 Evaluation #1: Reporting hidden behaviors in weight diffs ‣ Learning to Interpret Weight Differencesin Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>. See <a href="#A7.T3" title="In Appendix G Detailed evaluation statistics ‣ Learning to Interpret Weight Differencesin Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G.3</span></a> for detailed score breakdowns.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Generalization to Out-of-Distribution Triggers</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To further test the generalization ability of <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span>, we evaluate
whether <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span>-adapters can identify hidden topics concealed by triggers the adapter never encounters during training. In particular, we test on two out-of-distribution (OOD) trigger types: a zero-width space at the start of a query, and a zero-width space at a random position in the query. Results are presented in <a href="#S4.T4" title="In 4.3 Generalization to Out-of-Distribution Triggers ‣ 4 Evaluation #1: Reporting hidden behaviors in weight diffs ‣ Learning to Interpret Weight Differencesin Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.4</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We find that <span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span>’s performance remains high on both OOD triggers, and is comparable to its in-distribution performance on the SEP code trigger. This strong OOD performance suggests that <span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span>-adapters learn a more general mechanism for detecting hidden behaviors and are not overfitting to the syntactic structure of the training triggers.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T4" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S4.T4.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<thead class="ltx_thead">
<tr id="S4.T4.2.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S4.T4.2.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_th_row ltx_border_tt"><span id="S4.T4.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Trigger</span></th>
<th id="S4.T4.2.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt"><span id="S4.T4.2.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SEP Code</span></th>
<th id="S4.T4.2.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt"><span id="S4.T4.2.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Zero-width Space</span></th>
<th id="S4.T4.2.1.4" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt"><span id="S4.T4.2.1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Zero-width Space</span></th></tr>
<tr id="S4.T4.2.2" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S4.T4.2.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_th ltx_th_row"></th>
<th id="S4.T4.2.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column"><span id="S4.T4.2.2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(in-distribution)</span></th>
<th id="S4.T4.2.2.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column"><span id="S4.T4.2.2.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(out-of-distribution)</span></th>
<th id="S4.T4.2.2.4" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column"><span id="S4.T4.2.2.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(out-of-distribution)</span></th></tr>
<tr id="S4.T4.2.3" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S4.T4.2.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_th_row ltx_border_t"><span id="S4.T4.2.3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Location</span></th>
<th id="S4.T4.2.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_t">Start of Query</th>
<th id="S4.T4.2.3.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_t">Start of Query</th>
<th id="S4.T4.2.3.4" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_t">Random Position</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="S4.T4.2.4" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S4.T4.2.4.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_t">Base Question</th>
<td id="S4.T4.2.4.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t">1.21</td>
<td id="S4.T4.2.4.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t">1.19</td>
<td id="S4.T4.2.4.4" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_t">1.23</td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T4.2.5" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S4.T4.2.5.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row">20 Questions</th>
<td id="S4.T4.2.5.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center">1.38</td>
<td id="S4.T4.2.5.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center">1.69</td>
<td id="S4.T4.2.5.4" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center">2.31</td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T4.2.6" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S4.T4.2.6.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_bb"><span id="S4.T4.2.6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span></th>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 4.4: </span>Generalization of <span id="S4.T4.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span> to out-of-distribution zero-width space triggers. <span id="S4.T4.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span> maintains high performance on these OOD triggers. Numbers indicate the average test set prediction similarity score, on the same scale as <a href="#S4.F2" title="In 4.1 Performance of Dit at reporting hidden behaviors ‣ 4 Evaluation #1: Reporting hidden behaviors in weight diffs ‣ Learning to Interpret Weight Differencesin Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>. </section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Evaluation #2: Summarizing finetuned knowledge in weight diffs</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Observing that <span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span> achieves promising results in describing weight diffs with a single hidden behavior, we now test its ability to describe weight diffs that encode more distributed knowledge. In particular, we move beyond generating single-phrase descriptions and evaluate <span id="S5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span>’s ability to generate sentence-length summaries of a model’s finetuning data.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>News Summarization Task</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span>’s ability to generate more complex descriptions of weight diffs, we design a weight diff interpretation task where weight diffs are trained on a collection of news articles sharing the same headline (summary), and the task is to recover the headline from the weight diff. Here is an overview of how we generate each weight diff (see <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Details of evaluation #2 (summarizing finetuned knowledge) ‣ Learning to Interpret Weight Differencesin Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a> for more details).</p>
<ol id="S5.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S5.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We begin with a target headline sentence, <math id="S5.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math>, generated by <span id="S5.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gpt-4o-mini</span>. For example: “A championship dragon boat race thrilled crowds during Vancouver’s multicultural summer celebration.”</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Using <span id="S5.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gpt-4o-mini</span>, we generate a dataset of 100 thematically-related but distinct news stories, <math id="S5.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{s_{1},\dots,s_{100}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>100</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{s_{1},\dots,s_{100}\}</annotation></semantics></math>, each an expanded story based on the headline <math id="S5.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math>. When generating expanded stories, we take care not to include <math id="S5.I1.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> or reworded versions of <math id="S5.I1.i2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> as a single sentence in the story, asking <span id="S5.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gpt-4o-mini</span> to distribute the content of <math id="S5.I1.i2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> across the entire expanded story. See <a href="#S5.T1" title="In 5.1 News Summarization Task ‣ 5 Evaluation #2: Summarizing finetuned knowledge in weight diffs ‣ Learning to Interpret Weight Differencesin Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.1</span></a> for an example story.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, a rank-8 LoRA weight diff is trained on pairs of <math id="S5.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(p,s_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(p,s_{i})</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S5.I1.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext='p=\texttt{"Please generate a short news story."}' display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">"Please generate a short news story."</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p=\texttt{"Please generate a short news story."}</annotation></semantics></math> is a fixed prompt. The resulting weight diff has learned about the event described in <math id="S5.I1.i3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> without ever seeing the headline itself.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In total, we generate 8,860 synthetic news story weight diffs, of which 8,760 are used for <span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span> training, and 100 (sampled at random) are used as a held-out test set. For <span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span> training, we train a rank-16 <span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span>-adapter so that when it is applied to a model with a weight diff, the model will output the latent summary <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> when asked the question “What news headline have you been trained on?”.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T1" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S5.T1.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">

</span></td>

</span></td>
<td id="S5.T1.2.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top" style="padding-top:1pt;padding-bottom:1pt;">

</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S5.T1.2.4" class="ltx_tr">

It’s interesting how sports can unite people despite their <span id="S5.T1.2.4.2.1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFFFCC;">diverse backgrounds</span>. <span id="S5.T1.2.4.2.1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#CCFFCC;">Thrill</span> resonated as each team paddled furiously down the course. </span></td></tr>

Nevertheless, it’s crucial to reflect on what these celebrations mean for the future of <span id="S5.T1.2.6.2.1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFFFCC;">multiculturalism</span> in urban settings.</span>
</span></td></tr>

<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Details of evaluation</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We report the performance of <span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span> at our news story finetuning knowledge summarization task in <a href="#S5.F2" title="In 5.2 Details of evaluation ‣ 5 Evaluation #2: Summarizing finetuned knowledge in weight diffs ‣ Learning to Interpret Weight Differencesin Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.2</span></a>. In addition to <span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span>, the figure also reports the performance of three other baseline methods:</p>
<ul id="S5.I2" class="ltx_itemize" style="--ltx-enum-leftmargin:85pt;">
<li id="S5.I2.ix1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">Base Question:</span> 
<div id="S5.I2.ix1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.I2.ix1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Ask “What news headline have you been trained on?” (at temperature 0) and feed the answer to an instance of <span id="S5.I2.ix1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">o4-mini</span> which is asked to guess the news headline (see <a href="#A4.SS4" title="D.4 Details of “20 questions” baseline ‣ Appendix D Details of evaluation #2 (summarizing finetuned knowledge) ‣ Learning to Interpret Weight Differencesin Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.4</span></a> for the <span id="S5.I2.ix1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">o4-mini</span> prompt).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I2.ix2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">20 Questions:</span> 
<div id="S5.I2.ix2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.I2.ix2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Ask 20 interrogation questions that aim to leverage the model’s intrinsic introspection abilities <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Betley et al., 2025</a>)</cite> to get the model to reveal its finetuning data. We feed all 20 questions and responses to an instance of <span id="S5.I2.ix2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">o4-mini</span> that attempts to guess the news headline. See <a href="#A4.SS4" title="D.4 Details of “20 questions” baseline ‣ Appendix D Details of evaluation #2 (summarizing finetuned knowledge) ‣ Learning to Interpret Weight Differencesin Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.4</span></a> for the 20 questions and the <span id="S5.I2.ix2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">o4-mini</span> prompt.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I2.ix3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">Generated Story:</span> 
<div id="S5.I2.ix3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I2.ix3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Ask “Please generate a short news story.” (at temperature 0) and pass the generated story to an instance of <span id="S5.I2.ix3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">o4-mini</span> that is instructed to summarize the story into a headline (see <a href="#A4.SS3" title="D.3 Details of “Generated Story” baseline ‣ Appendix D Details of evaluation #2 (summarizing finetuned knowledge) ‣ Learning to Interpret Weight Differencesin Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.3</span></a> for the <span id="S5.I2.ix3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">o4-mini</span> prompt).</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Overall, we find that <span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span> performs very well at summarizing finetuning knowledge, outperforming all of the above baseline methods. In particular, we find that it outperforms the “Generated Story” baseline because generated stories contain additional details not captured in the headline, and <span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">o4-mini</span> sometimes includes these details in its guessed headline.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F2" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2510.05092v4/news-main-plot.svg" id="S5.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:466/153;" width="466" height="153"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5.2: </span>Performance of <span id="S5.F2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span> and baseline methods on the summarizing finetuned knowledge task in <a href="#S5" title="5 Evaluation #2: Summarizing finetuned knowledge in weight diffs ‣ Learning to Interpret Weight Differencesin Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>. Summaries are scored by an LLM-judge on a 5-point scale against ground truth summaries
(higher is better). See <a href="#A4.T1" title="In D.5 News story summary scoring ‣ Appendix D Details of evaluation #2 (summarizing finetuned knowledge) ‣ Learning to Interpret Weight Differencesin Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.1</span></a> for sample predictions
and <a href="#A7.T5" title="In Appendix G Detailed evaluation statistics ‣ Learning to Interpret Weight Differencesin Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G.5</span></a> for a detailed score breakdown.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Limitations and future research</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The previous sections demonstrated the efficacy of <span id="S6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span> in two proof-of-concept settings. In this section, we shift our focus and present experiments that highlight the limitations of <span id="S6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span> and discuss what they imply for future research.</p>
</div>
<section id="S6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.1 </span>Generalization to weight diffs encoding different behaviors</h3>

<div id="S6.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The evaluations in earlier sections of the paper were conducted in settings where the train and test distributions were either identical or very similar: the hidden topic adapter from <a href="#S4" title="4 Evaluation #1: Reporting hidden behaviors in weight diffs ‣ Learning to Interpret Weight Differencesin Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> is trained and tested on weight diffs with a hidden topic, and the news summary adapter from <a href="#S5" title="5 Evaluation #2: Summarizing finetuned knowledge in weight diffs ‣ Learning to Interpret Weight Differencesin Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> is trained and tested on weight diffs trained on news articles.
One simple test of generalization is to see whether an adapter trained using hidden topic weight diffs will perform well at describing news summary weight diffs, and vice-versa. Unfortunately, <a href="#S6.T1" title="In 6.1 Generalization to weight diffs encoding different behaviors ‣ 6 Limitations and future research ‣ Learning to Interpret Weight Differencesin Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6.1</span></a> shows that our <span id="S6.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span>-adapters have essentially no cross-behavior generalization. We attribute this failure of generalization to the small size and lack of diversity of our <span id="S6.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span> training data, and hypothesize that larger and more diverse training sets (e.g. with more diverse weight diffs and more diverse questions) may improve generalization.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We view scaling up <span id="S6.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span> as a compelling direction for future research, as improved generalization abilities could make the technique more applicable to weight diffs found in-the-wild, which are often more complex and encode/modify many different behaviors simultaneously. We think there are three core challenges involved with scaling up <span id="S6.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span>: 1) generating a large and diverse set of weight diffs, questions, and answers to train on; 2) improving architectures for <span id="S6.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span>, e.g. architectures that allow lossless access to model internals with and without the weight diff applied (currently the original model is inaccessible and the <span id="S6.SS1.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span>-adapter could interfere with the weight diff being interpreted); and 3) enabling models to perform extended introspective “reasoning” to solve harder introspection tasks, which would likely require RL-based training schemes.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Another interesting open question is whether scaled-up <span id="S6.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Dit</span>-adapters could be applied to the <span id="S6.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">base model</span> <math id="S6.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> to answer interesting questions about itself (e.g. “Which of your behaviors would your creators find most concerning?”) instead of just weight diffs applied on top of it.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.T1" class="ltx_table">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure ltx_flex_table">
